cells.tense: You are already deciding this, with the pen down and the page moving under it.
cells.ask: Say the choice out loud to one person today, in the plain words you'd use alone. No case for it, no explaining the reasoning.
cells.core:
You don't build a case and then move. The read lands whole and the moving happens with it — by the time you could explain it, the choice is already made. That isn't haste. The structure underneath is complete enough to move without asking permission from anyone, including you.

What carries it is a settled read. You take in enough that the next thing simply follows. Most people call that certainty, and it isn't. It's knowing that can wait — you can hold something true for a while before you say it, and the waiting does useful work.

But you sit on it longer than the room needs. Name it plainly to someone, once, and let that be the whole of it.
cells.sheetLine: Decisions arrive complete with you, and the moving follows.

cells.tense: You are living a few moves ahead, in a room that hasn't been built yet.
cells.ask: Put the plan down in a short note, then close it and spend ten minutes doing something with your hands. The break is the practice.
cells.core:
You're not asserting anything. You're running every possible version at once — the one that derails here, the one that stalls there — and the running has become the place you live, ahead of the conversation you're in.

Out ahead the structure feels total, so each exchange turns into a chance to install it. But you're steering toward a room that hasn't been built, and the consequences you're bracing for are ones you invented. Other people don't get to be in the decision with you, and the decision doesn't get to meet the room it was actually for.

This isn't about going easy. Bring the read back to what's in front of you, then leave it standing.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that's already behind you, holding the handle.
cells.ask: Make one small call today — dinner, a time, which way to walk — and write it beside your own name. One line, and it's finished.
cells.core:
When this is working, you take in enough that direction is obvious. The read arrives and the moving comes with it, no argument needed. What shows up instead is waiting — for the pull to arrive from somewhere else and confirm itself, which it doesn't, and so nothing begins.

You can already say what's true. The sentence is sitting right there, complete. You just aren't the one who gets to have said it, and that's the difference between knowing the way and taking it.

Don't try to direct harder. Finish one small thing from plans that are already solid, put your name on it, and let the finished piece show you what your own say-so feels like. One piece is enough.
cells.sheetLine: The read is there. The starting isn't coming from you.

cells.tense: You are holding the pen and writing in a room you believe someone else furnished.
cells.ask: Pick one decision you're carrying — the shape of your week, a call you make — and say to yourself what you're choosing there. Once, plainly, no audience.
cells.core:
You're already directing this. It shows in what you let pass, what you take seriously, the way things move when nobody has said a word about direction. But in your own account it happened by itself — the work lined up, the timing worked out, someone else set the course.

The directing is doing real work. It shapes what the people around you take as settled. Nobody's asking you to prove it, and nobody's asking you to be louder. The plain sentence is still sitting undrafted, and has been for a while now.

This isn't about deciding harder. Put the plain word on one decision you're making and keeping, so the standing has somewhere to land.
cells.sheetLine: The steering is happening. Your name isn't on it yet.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is in Too Little: I write 'somewhere you stopped saying it out loud' as if I know they stopped, when the record only says the seat is under-expressed and past-anchored. Let me narrow it to what shows and let the reader object: 'you've stopped' becomes 'the moving isn't the part that's stuck.' The reader could reasonably say the door image at the close of Too Little is biographical — so it names no room, no person, no year, only the posture of standing at a threshold that has already passed. The ask survives my being wrong at every status: each one is a small physical act with a finish (write the sentence, say it once, make the one call, let papers stay unsorted) that teaches something about where direction actually sits even if the read is off. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you don't need the assertion' — it's a line about being impressive, so I've replaced it with what clarity costs a person who has already decided.
